041.subtitle: The axe laid to the forest of becoming

commentary.meaning: The ascent through the cakras is over and the hymn changes its manner. What follows for many verses is arranged by sound rather than by subject, and this verse opens the run of names beginning in bha-. The syllable is turned over three times in three unrelated senses. She is Bhavānī, wife of Bhava, which is one of the oldest names of Rudra. She is reached by bhāvanā, the mind's sustained holding of a thing until it is present — a different word that only sounds like the first. Then bhava means what it means in ordinary religious speech, the world one is born into over and over, and she is the small axe taken to its trunks. A husband, a discipline and a forest being felled, all out of one syllable. The verse then turns to bhadra, the auspicious, and states it twice: what she loves is the good, and her own shape is the good. It closes by saying what she does with it. Saubhāgya is not earned by those who receive it; it is handed to them.
commentary.history:
The eleven names before this one climbed the six cakras and ended with kuṇḍalinī herself, finer than a lotus fibre. From bhavānī onward the governing consideration is no longer subject but sound. Names in bha- run from here to bhayāpahā; the sibilants take over at śāmbhavī and hold until śāntimatī; the long negative series in ni- begins at nirādhārā and does not release for fifty-six names; then come the names in dur-, then those in sarva-, and then a block of nearly thirty beginning mahā-. Nothing of the sort happens in the first hundred names, which follow her body from crown to foot and then the war with Bhaṇḍāsura in narrative order. Having finished describing her, the Vāgdevatās begin sorting her, and they sort by ear. This is worth knowing before starting the next fifteen verses, because it explains why names that have nothing to do with each other stand side by side, and why a name about her waist can appear in the middle of a page of metaphysics.

Bhava is Vedic. In the Śatarudrīya, the litany of Rudra's names in the Yajurveda, Bhava and Śarva stand together in the same breath of salutation, and both will be used here within twelve names of each other. Later systematisers gathered eight such names into the aṣṭamūrti scheme, the eight forms in which Śiva is said to stand as the elements, the luminaries and the sacrificer. What matters for this verse is only that Bhava is the name of Rudra taken as the source of coming-to-be — bhava from the root bhū, to become — so that Bhavānī is the feminine of becoming itself, and the name that immediately follows can play on the same root without changing the subject.

The suffix is worth a moment because Pāṇini legislates for it by name. Sūtra 4.1.49 lists the words that take the augment ānuk before the feminine ending: indra, varuṇa, bhava, śarva, rudra, mṛḍa, hima, araṇya, yava, yavana, mātula, ācārya. That is why we have indrāṇī, rudrāṇī, mṛḍānī, and here bhavānī and śarvāṇī. The grammar is not decoration: three of the twelve stems on Pāṇini's list turn up as names of this goddess's husband in these two verses.

Bhāvanā is the technical term of the pair. It is the causative of the same root — a making-to-be, the mind's power of bringing a thing into presence rather than merely thinking about it. In this tradition it has a text of its own. The Bhāvana Upaniṣad, a short Śākta upaniṣad attached to the Atharvaveda and the subject of a commentary by Bhāskararāya, teaches the internal worship in which the Śrīcakra is identified point by point with the practitioner's own body and faculties, so that the entire ritual can be performed without a diagram, a lamp or an offering. To call her bhāvanāgamyā is to say that this is the road that arrives, and that the external apparatus, however elaborate, is a means to it and not a substitute for it.

The forest is a standing image. Saṃsāra grows like scrub — dense, self-seeding, impossible to see out of — and Indian religious literature has been cutting it down for a very long time; the Bhagavad Gītā's aśvattha, rooted upward and impossible to trace to its beginning, is felled with the firm axe of non-attachment. What is peculiar to this name is the size of the tool. Kuṭhārikā is a diminutive: not the great war-axe of Paraśurāma but a hatchet, a woman's small axe, and grammatically feminine. The Śrīvidyā tradition has its own connection with the axe-bearer, since one of its principal ritual manuals is the Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra, but this name is not reaching for grandeur. A whole forest, and one small blade.

Bhadra and saubhāgya close the verse and they are not the same idea. Bhadra is the plain old Vedic word for what is good and auspicious, the word in the prayer that we may hear what is bhadra with our ears. Saubhāgya is narrower and much more loaded: it is the good fortune specifically of the married woman, and in this tradition it is the name of the school itself. Bhāskararāya called his commentary on this stotra the Saubhāgyabhāskara; the vidyā is called saubhāgyavidyā; the goddess is Saubhāgyasundarī. So the last name of the verse says, quietly, that what she gives her devotees is her own tradition's name for grace.
commentary.practice:
The first two names are a vowel-length drill of the purest kind, and getting them wrong is the commonest mistake in this verse. Bhavānī is short-long-long: bha-vā-nī. Bhāvanā is long-short-long: bhā-va-nā. The lengths are exchanged between one word and the next, and the metre will not forgive it. Say them slowly as a pair, three or four times, until the ear can hear which syllable is carrying weight.

There are seven aspirated bh sounds in these thirty-two syllables and every one of them must be heard as b followed by a breath, not as an English v and not as a bare b. Bhavānī, bhāvanā, bhava, bhadra, bhadra, bhakta, saubhāgya. Say bha with the lips closed, then released with a puff. A verse this heavily alliterated is exactly where the aspiration tends to be dropped, because the mouth starts taking shortcuts.

The nasal contrast is the second drill. Bhavānī and bhāvanā take the dental n, tongue-tip forward against the upper teeth. Bhavāraṇya takes the retroflex ṇ, tongue-tip curled back to the hard palate, and it comes wrapped in a conjunct: ṇya, retroflex nasal followed by y. The r earlier in the word is what has pulled that n backwards, and the same thing will happen to śarvāṇī two verses from now, while bhavānī keeps its dental n because there is no r in bhava. One rule, two names, an audible difference.

Kuṭhārikā holds the other hard sound: ṭh is the retroflex t with aspiration, tongue-tip curled back and released with breath. It is not the th of English think, which does not exist in Sanskrit at all. Take the word as ku-ṭhā-ri-kā and let the ā ring.

One piece of written sandhi to see. The second line reads bhadramūrtir bhakta-, but the name is bhadramūrtiḥ, ending in a visarga. Before the voiced bh of the next word the visarga has become r, and the Devanagari joins them into मूर्तिर्भक्त. The same thing will happen at mahālakṣmīr and mahābuddhir later in this batch, so it is worth registering now: when a name ending in -iḥ is followed by a voiced sound, the visarga you would expect at a pause turns into an r inside the line.

The rest is straightforward. Saubhāgya has the diphthong au, then bh, then the conjunct gy — three separate difficulties in one word, and the usual failure is to swallow the g. Bhadra and priyā give you dr and pr, both with a fully trilled or tapped r.

Metrically this is a plain anuṣṭubh, eight syllables to the quarter, and the names fall into it neatly: three plus five in the first quarter, then a single eight-syllable name, then four plus four, then another eight. Breathe after kuṭhārikā, at the halfway point.

For what to hold while chanting: the three senses of bhava in the first line are not a pun for its own sake. Read as a sequence they say that the god of becoming, the discipline that makes a thing present, and the thicket one is lost in are all approached through the same door. And the closing name is the one to rest on if the verse is used alone. It says that the fortune in question is given, not achieved, which is the note the whole of the next verse will develop.

commentary.meaning: Four names on devotion and then, in the middle of the verse, a change of consonant. The four are graded and the grading is the point. First devotion is what she likes best of everything offered to her; then it is the road that actually arrives, where learning and ritual only go part of the way; and then, in the boldest of the three, it is what has power over her — vaśya is the word used of a thing brought under control, and the goddess is the object. Having conceded that much she is said to carry fear away, which is the natural consequence: there is nothing left to be afraid of in someone who has agreed to be governed. Then the sibilants take over and the register shifts from what she does for the devotee to who she is beside her husband. Śambhu's power, Śarva's wife, worshipped by the goddess of speech herself, and a giver of śarman — a word that means shelter first and the ease of being sheltered second.
commentary.history:
The three bhakti names are not synonyms padded out to fill a line. Priyā, gamyā and vaśyā make a ladder, and each rung concedes more. That she is fond of devotion is unremarkable; every devotional text says as much, and the Gītā says it in its most quoted form when it accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water offered with love. That she is reached by devotion is a stronger claim, because it puts bhakti above the two rivals a Sanskrit text would name in the same breath, knowledge and ritual action; the Gītā again makes precisely this move at the end of its eleventh chapter, where the vision of the universal form is said to be available by undivided devotion and by nothing else, not the four Vedas, not austerity, not gift, not sacrifice. But bhaktivaśyā goes past both. Vaśya belongs to the vocabulary of control. In tantric ritual manuals vaśīkaraṇa is one of the six acts, the rite by which a practitioner brings another person under his will, and it is named alongside pacification, immobilisation and worse. To call the goddess vaśyā is to say that the one thing which works on her is the one thing that cannot be performed as a technique.

Bhayāpahā closes the set and closes it correctly. Fear is what the ritual manuals are mostly about — the six acts exist because the world is dangerous — and a goddess who has already conceded that devotion governs her has nothing left to threaten anyone with.

With śāmbhavī the hymn turns to the husband's names, and it takes them from the oldest available stock. Śambhu means the one who is good to be with, from śam, wellbeing, and bhū; it is the mildest of Śiva's names, the one used when the terrifying aspect is being deliberately set aside. Śāmbhavī is its feminine derivative and it is also a technical term with a long history: śāmbhavī mudrā is the yogic posture of the eyes open and the attention withdrawn, and in the non-dual Śaivism of Kashmir the śāmbhava upāya is the highest of the three paths, the one in which nothing whatever is done because there is no distance left to cross. The name carries that sense as well as the marital one.

Śarvāṇī takes the other Vedic name. Śarva and Bhava stand side by side in the Śatarudrīya, and the ancient sense of śarva is the archer, the one whose arrow is out; the name is old enough that the Atharvaveda tradition treats Śarva as a distinct being to be placated rather than a title of anyone. Set beside bhavānī in the previous verse it completes a pair the Veda itself had already made.

Śāradārādhyā is the odd one out and the most interesting. Śāradā is Sarasvatī under her autumn name, the goddess of speech and learning, and she is here not among the worshipped but among the worshippers. This should be read against the frame narrative of the stotra itself, in which the thousand names are not composed by a human seer but by the Vāgdevatās, the goddesses of speech headed by Vaśinī, on Lalitā's own command. The hymn has already told us that speech worships her. This name says it again in a single word. It is also the name that ties the text to a place: Śāradā is the presiding goddess of the Śṛṅgeri maṭha and of the Śāradā Pīṭha in Kashmir, and Śrīvidyā in South India has been transmitted in institutions that worship her.

Śarmadāyinī ends the verse on another Vedic word. Śarman is a shelter, a roof, a covering — the Ṛgveda asks constantly for śarman, meaning literally a place to be under during a storm — and only by extension does it come to mean happiness. It is also the ending traditionally attached to brahmin personal names. The verse that began by admitting that devotion controls her ends by saying that what she hands out is a roof.
commentary.practice:
The first line repeats bhakti- three times and the temptation is to let the repetitions blur into each other. They should not. Each is four syllables, bhak-ti-pri-yā, bhak-ti-gam-yā, bhak-ti-vaś-yā, and the whole information of the line is in the fourth syllable of each: -yā preceded by pri, gam, vaś. Chant the line with the second element slightly deliberate and the ladder becomes audible.

The cluster kt in bhakti is a dental t immediately after an unaspirated k, with no vowel between them. English has the sequence only across word boundaries. Say bhak and then ti as two closed gestures rather than gliding. Vaśyā adds the palatal ś before y, both made at the hard palate, so the tongue does not move between them.

The second line is one long exercise in the palatal sibilant. Śāmbhavī, śāradārādhyā, śarvāṇī, śarmadāyinī: four names, four ś sounds, and not one of them is the s of English see. The tongue-body rises to the hard palate, as it does for the y of yes, and the air hisses over it. Do this four times and the line is nearly finished.

Śāmbhavī hides a conjunct that most reciters simplify. It is m followed by aspirated bh: śām-bha-vī, with the lips closing for the m and reopening with a breath for the bh. Śāradārādhyā ends in dhy, a voiced aspirated dental followed by y, and it is preceded by three long ā vowels in a row — śā-ra-dā-rā-dhyā — which is the sort of run that makes reciters hurry. Do not.

The finest point in the verse is the pair śarvāṇī and śarmadāyinī. The first has a retroflex ṇ, the second a dental n, and they are three syllables apart. The reason is a rule of the language: an r earlier in the word pulls a following n back to the retroflex position, provided nothing that blocks the process intervenes. In śarvāṇī the intervening v does not block it, so the n retroflexes. In bhavānī of the previous verse there is no r at all, so it stays dental. In mṛḍānī, which is not in the text but is the same formation from mṛḍa, the retroflex ḍ does block it and the n stays dental too. That is a real grammatical mechanism producing an audible difference, and this pair of verses puts both outcomes within a few seconds of each other.

One more small thing: bhayāpahā is bhaya plus apahā, and the a of bhaya has merged with the a of apahā into a single long ā. The word is four syllables, bha-yā-pa-hā, and the long second syllable is the seam.

Metrically the verse divides cleanly into eight four-syllable names, two per quarter, with the natural breath after bhayāpahā. It is one of the easiest verses in the stotra to memorise for exactly that reason, and it is often used as the entry point by people learning the hymn.

For contemplation the third name is the one to sit with. It is a strange thing for a hymn to say of its own deity that she can be controlled, and the tradition does not soften it. The instruction hidden in the order of the four names is that the only leverage anyone has on her is the one that cannot be manufactured — which is why the fourth name can promise the end of fear without sounding like a boast.

043.subtitle: The autumn moon, and then the turn to nothing

commentary.meaning: The sibilant run finishes and the hymn pivots. Six names carry on in the manner of the last verse — Śaṅkara's own, maker of prosperity, the virtuous one, her face the autumn moon, her waist drawn thin, possessed of peace — and they are the ordinary currency of praise poetry: a husband's name, a benefit, a moral quality, a simile, a body part. Then the last two names of the verse do something the hymn has not done before. Nirādhārā and nirañjanā are both formed by negation, and after them the stotra will not stop negating for fifty-six names. The hinge is placed with some care. Śāntimatī, possessed of peace, still describes her as having something. Nirādhārā says she has no support, which after the cakra verses is pointed, since she was called the one whose single dwelling is the root support only thirty-three names ago. Nirañjanā says nothing takes on her at all. The verse begins by comparing her face to the moon and ends by saying that she has no surface for a comparison to stick to.
commentary.history:
Śaṅkara is the name of Śiva as the one who makes things well, from śam and the root kṛ, and it is also of course the name of the philosopher whom tradition credits with the Saundaryalaharī and with the reconciliation of Advaita Vedānta and goddess worship on which Śrīvidyā depends. Whether Śaṅkarācārya wrote that poem is doubtful and has been doubted for a long time, but the association is old and it is part of why this stotra can move, as it is about to, from erotic simile to unqualified negation without any sense of changing subject. Śrīkarī, immediately after, is the counterweight: the maker of śrī, of splendour and prosperity and Lakṣmī's own quality, which is the word the first three names of the whole stotra were built on.

Sādhvī is the only plainly moral epithet in this stretch and the only name in the line that begins with a dental s rather than a palatal ś. It means straight, true, good — from the root sādh, to succeed or to bring to completion — and in ordinary usage it is what one calls a virtuous woman. Placed among names for the wife of Śaṅkara and the maker of fortune, it insists that the goddess is also simply good in the domestic and social sense, which a tradition with the reputation Śrīvidyā has needs to say from time to time and does say, repeatedly, in its most public texts.

The two physical names are worth pausing over because they arrive out of order. The head-to-foot description of her body finished long ago, around the fiftieth name, and the hymn has since covered the mantra, the cakras and the ascent of kuṇḍalinī. Now, in the middle of an alphabetical run, her face and her waist reappear, and another such intrusion is coming at nīlacikurā seven verses from now. This is not carelessness. The alliterative principle governing this stretch throws up whatever names begin with the right sound, and the composers evidently preferred to keep the body present rather than to let the hymn become an argument. The comparison itself is the oldest in the language: śarat is autumn, the season after the monsoon has washed the sky, when the moon is at its clearest, and śaraccandra is the standard against which faces are measured from the Rāmāyaṇa onward. Śātodarī, thin-bellied, belongs to the same conventional repertoire.

Then the turn. Nirādhārā means without a support, and ādhāra is not a vague word in this hymn: at name ninety-nine she was mūlādhāraikanilayā, she whose one dwelling is the root support, the lowest of the cakras. The tradition reads the present name as saying that she is the ground and therefore stands on nothing, which is the answer the Chāndogya Upaniṣad gives when the question is put directly and the pupil is told that the infinite rests in its own greatness, or perhaps not even in that. Much later in the stotra, at name six hundred and fifty-nine, she is called sarvādhārā, the support of everything. The negation here and the affirmation there are the same statement made twice, and the whole architecture of the next thirteen verses works that way.

Nirañjanā is the heavier of the two. Añjana is what you smear on — collyrium for the eyes, ointment, pigment — and by extension any taint or colouring. Nirañjana is one of the most widely used words in Indian religious vocabulary for the unstained absolute; the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad uses it of the knower who has shaken off both merit and demerit, and the Śvetāśvatara puts it in a list of five epithets of which four will turn up as names in the next six verses of this stotra. The haṭha yoga texts use nirañjana as one of the synonyms for the state of samādhi. When the sahasranāma reaches for the word it is not coining anything; it is stepping into a vocabulary that the upaniṣads, the Vedāntins, the Śaivas and the yogins had all been using for centuries, and it is announcing, at the end of a verse about a moonlike face and a slender waist, that everything said so far is going to be taken back.
commentary.practice:
The first line contains all three Sanskrit sibilants in the space of ten syllables and it is the best drill in this batch. Śāṅkarī and śrīkarī open with the palatal ś, tongue-body against the hard palate. Sādhvī opens with the dental s, tongue-tip forward at the teeth. Then śaraccandra returns to the palatal. Three names, ś ś s ś, and if the difference is not being made the line collapses into an undifferentiated hiss.

Śāṅkarī has the guttural nasal ṅ before k, made right at the back where the k is made; the tongue never leaves that position between the two sounds. Śrīkarī opens with śr, palatal sibilant into r, which is the same cluster as the śrī that opens the whole stotra. Sādhvī puts a voiced aspirated dh in front of v: sā-dhvī, two syllables, and the aspiration must be heard.

Śaraccandranibhānanā holds the verse's best sandhi. The first element is śarat, autumn, ending in a dental t. Before the palatal c of candra that t has itself become a palatal and doubled, so śarat plus candra gives śaraccandra, written with c and c joined. This is a rule you will meet everywhere once you have seen it: a final t assimilates to a following palatal. Say it as śa-rac-can-dra, letting the doubled consonant have its full length, and the metre will come out right. The rest of the name is three dental nasals in a row across nibhānanā — ni-bhā-na-nā — with an aspirated bh in the middle.

Śātodarī has a dental t, not a retroflex one, which surprises people who expect a retroflex after the long ā. Śāntimatī has the dental cluster nt. Neither is difficult, but both are places where a reciter drifting on autopilot will start curling the tongue back out of habit, because the retroflexes are coming.

The last two names are where the verse changes character and the mouth should register it. Nirādhārā is four open syllables with an aspirated dh in the middle and nothing to trip on. Nirañjanā has ñj, the palatal nasal followed by the palatal j, and it is one of the sounds English speakers habitually replace with the n of ninja, which is close but made further forward. Put the tongue-body where it goes for y, keep it there, and let the j come off the same surface.

Metrically the first quarter is unusually crowded — three names in eight syllables, three plus three plus two — and then a single eight-syllable name fills the second. The second line is four names of four syllables each. Breathe after śaraccandranibhānanā.

For what to hold: this is the verse where the hymn turns, and it is worth chanting the two halves with different weight. The first six names are praise of a kind anyone can follow. The last two withdraw the ground from under them. The traditional counsel for the long negative series that follows is not to treat it as philosophy being recited but as a series of removals actually being performed, one name at a time, and this verse is where the first two are taken away.

commentary.meaning: Ten names in thirty-two syllables, the densest verse in the hymn so far, and eight of the ten are removals. Nothing adheres to her; no dirt marks her; she has no outline that could be drawn; nothing crowds or scatters her; the three strands out of which nature is woven do not run through her; she does not come in portions; she wants nothing; no disaster reaches her. Two of the ten are stated positively, and they are placed where the metre can hold them — nityā at the end of the first quarter and śāntā at the end of the third, each of them two syllables, each closing a line of four-beat names like a rest in a bar. What the verse never does is sort its negations. Stain and agitation are defects and could in principle be removed from anyone; parts, shape and the three strands are not defects at all but the constituents of everything that exists. The hymn takes them away in the same breath and in the same grammatical form, and the refusal to distinguish is the argument.
commentary.history:
The scale of what has just begun is worth stating plainly. From nirādhārā at the end of the last verse to niratyayā seven verses from now, fifty-six consecutive names run without a break in the pattern. Forty-four of them begin with the syllable ni. Eleven of the remaining twelve are the paired destroyer-names that answer a negative name in the same line — rāgamathanī after nīrāgā, pāpanāśinī after niṣpāpā, and so on. Exactly one name in the whole stretch stands entirely outside the scheme, and it is śāntā, in this verse. Nothing else in the thousand names is built like this.

The prefix doing the work is a single word wearing several faces. It is nis, and its final s behaves according to what follows: r before a vowel or a voiced consonant, ṣ before k, ś before c, plain s before t, a bare visarga before s, and nothing at all before r, where the loss is compensated by lengthening the i. Over the course of these seven verses the reciter will meet every one of those forms — nirlepā and nirguṇā here, niścintā later, niḥsaṃśayā, nīrāgā, nistulā. It is the same prefix throughout. The Devanagari changes shape; the meaning does not.

The vocabulary is not the hymn's own invention, and it is not vague. Almost every word in this verse and the next six has a settled home in the upaniṣads or in the philosophical schools. The clearest single witness is a verse near the end of the Śvetāśvatara that strings together five such epithets: partless, actionless, at peace, blameless, unstained. Every one of those five turns up as a name of Lalitā within seven verses of the present one — nirañjanā at a hundred and thirty-three, niṣkalā and śāntā here, niravadyā in the next verse, niṣkriyā five verses later. The Vāgdevatās are not paraphrasing Vedānta; they are taking its exact words and putting them in the feminine.

Nirguṇā is the load-bearing one. A guṇa is literally a strand of a rope, and in Sāṃkhya the three strands — sattva, rajas and tamas, clarity, motion and inertia — are what all of nature is twisted out of. To be nirguṇa is therefore not to be modest or unadorned but to be outside the material order altogether, and in Vedānta the word marks the highest of the standard distinctions: brahman with qualities, which can be worshipped, and brahman without them, which cannot. The Śvetāśvatara had already applied the word to a single god hidden in all beings, witness and knower, alone and without qualities. That a hymn of a thousand attributes should include the attribute of having none is a contradiction the tradition has never tried to hide. It is worth noting that the stotra makes no attempt to soften it either: seventy-seven names later she will be called mahāsattvā, of great sattva, and the two names stand in the same hymn without apology.

Niṣkalā is the other technical name here, and kalā is a rich word. It is a part, and specifically a sixteenth part; it is a digit of the moon; it is an art or a skill. In the Śaiva Āgamas the distinction between niṣkala and sakala is architectural before it is metaphysical: Śiva is worshipped as niṣkala in the plain liṅga with no features, as sakala in an image with face and limbs, and in an intermediate form in the liṅga that has a face carved on it. The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad had already used the word of brahman in the golden sheath, spotless and partless. And in this particular tradition the count of sixteen matters: there is a sixteen-syllabled form of the vidyā beyond the fifteen-syllabled one, and sixteen Nityā goddesses are worshipped in the Śrīcakra. A goddess whose school counts kalās so carefully is called, here, the one who has none.

The last name repays a look in the dictionary. Upaplava is any public calamity, an invasion, an inundation; Monier-Williams also gives it as a portent or natural phenomenon such as an eclipse, and as a name of Rāhu, the demon who swallows the moon. In a verse that has just called her partless — without kalās, without digits — the closing name can be heard as saying that this is the moon nothing ever eats. Whether the composers meant that cannot be known. That the language put it within reach is a fact about the language.
commentary.practice:
Ten names go past in ten seconds and the commonest failure here is not pronunciation but counting. Learn the shape first. The first quarter is three plus three plus two: nirlepā, nirmalā, nityā. The second quarter is two four-syllable names with a long ā in the second syllable, nirākārā and nirākulā, which is the only place in the verse where the rhythm opens out. The third quarter repeats the rhythm of the first exactly — nirguṇā, niṣkalā, śāntā — and the fourth is three plus five, niṣkāmā and nirupaplavā. Once the two short names ending the first and third quarters are fixed in the ear, the verse stops sliding.

The prefix is the pronunciation lesson. Say nir- with a full r before the voiced consonants of nirlepā, nirmalā, nirguṇā and before the vowel of nirākārā, nirākulā and nirupaplavā. Say niṣ-, with the retroflex sibilant, before the k of niṣkalā and niṣkāmā — the tongue-tip curls back for the ṣ and is already in position for nothing, since the k is made at the back, so the two must be given separately: niṣ, then kā. Learners regularly turn this into a plain s or into a sh made too far forward.

The retroflex ṇ of nirguṇā is not caused by the r. Guṇa has a retroflex ṇ of its own wherever it appears, and the same is true of the ṇ in kāraṇa in the next verse. Knowing which retroflexes are inherited and which are produced by a preceding r is the difference between remembering the sounds and understanding them.

Three clusters to isolate. Nirlepā has r running straight into l, two liquids with no vowel between them, and English speakers tend to insert one. Nityā is two syllables, nit-yā, with the t closing the first — not ni-ti-yā. Nirupaplavā ends in pl, and the whole word is five syllables of which only the last is long: ni-ru-pa-pla-vā. It is the lightest thing in the verse and should sound like it.

One long vowel to guard. Niṣkāmā has a long ā in the middle, because the word behind it is kāma; niṣkalā has a short a, because the word behind it is kalā. The two names are separated by only one other name and they are otherwise identical in shape. Getting the length wrong turns partless into desireless and back.

The verse is a plain anuṣṭubh and the breath goes after nirākulā. In the nāmāvalī form, where each name is turned into the dative for offering, this verse yields ten separate salutations — nirlepāyai namaḥ, nirmalāyai namaḥ, and so on — and it is worth performing once that way, slowly, because the archanā form makes it impossible to slur ten names into one gesture.

For what to hold while chanting: the tradition does not treat this stretch as doctrine being rehearsed. It treats it as a sequence of removals actually being carried out, and the instruction is to let each name take away what it names rather than to think about what it means. Ten names, ten things set down. The two that are stated positively, nityā and śāntā, are where the breath rests, and they are worth hearing as rests rather than as further claims.

045.subtitle: Forever pure, forever awake, forever free

commentary.meaning: Eight names, each of exactly four syllables, two to a quarter: the most regular verse in the stotra so far, and the regularity is audible. Three of the eight open with nitya, always, and they carry the weight. Her freedom is not an achievement but a standing condition, since she was never bound; her purity is not the result of washing; her wakefulness has no first moment. Between them sit four more removals — she does not alter, the spreading multiplicity of the world does not extend into her, she leans on nothing, there is no ledge in her for blame to grip — and the verse closes on the strangest of them. Nirantarā means without an interval: no gap in her anywhere, in space or in time, which is another way of saying that whatever is between two things is not between anything in her. Taken together the eight say one thing in eight ways, which is that nothing about her happened.
commentary.history:
Three of the four words in the standard Advaita formula for the nature of the self are here as names, and the fourth was two verses back. Śaṅkara opens his commentary on the Brahmasūtra by asserting that brahman exists, that its nature is eternal, pure, awake and free, that it is all-knowing and endowed with all powers. Nitya, śuddha, buddha, mukta: the phrase is a fixed unit in his prose and in the prose of everyone who came after him. This verse has nityamuktā, nityaśuddhā and nityabuddhā, and nityā itself stood at name one hundred and thirty-six. It is as close to a citation as an anuṣṭubh can come. And the remainder of Śaṅkara's sentence is not idle either: all-knowing and endowed with all powers will arrive as sarvajñā and sarvaśaktimayī in verses fifty-one and fifty-two, at the other end of this batch.

What the formula is doing is denying that liberation is an event. If purity had a date, something impure preceded it; if wakefulness began, there was sleep. The three nitya names refuse the date, and nityamuktā refuses it in the strongest place, since freedom is exactly what devotional and yogic literature normally describes as attained. Placed in a hymn addressed to a goddess who rose out of a fire-pit at a particular moment to kill a particular demon, the name is doing real work. The stotra means both things and does not reconcile them.

Nirvikārā takes a term from the analysis of causation. Vikāra is a modification, what a thing becomes when it changes without becoming another substance, and the classical statement is the Chāndogya's lesson about clay: knowing one lump of clay, everything made of clay is known, because the modification is a matter of speech and of naming, and the clay alone is real. To call her unchanging in that vocabulary is to place her on the side of the clay rather than of the pots.

Niṣprapañcā is the philosophically heaviest name in the verse. Prapañca is the spreading-out, the manifold, the world considered as multiplicity, and the word carries a note of proliferation rather than of mere plurality. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad's description of the fourth state — not conscious of the inner, not conscious of the outer, unseeable, ungraspable, unmarked, unthinkable — arrives at its climax with the phrase prapañcopaśamam, in which the spreading-out has subsided, followed at once by śāntam, at peace. Both of those are names in this stretch of the hymn. The Māṇḍūkya is the shortest of the classical upaniṣads and the one on which Advaita rests most heavily, and this name is a direct borrowing from its most quoted sentence.

Nirāśrayā looks at first like a repetition of nirādhārā from two verses ago, and commentators on this text spend a good deal of energy on such pairs. The distinction usually drawn is between a physical support underneath and a refuge one resorts to: an ādhāra holds something up, an āśraya is where something takes shelter. She has neither, and the second is the sharper claim, since the whole devotional apparatus of the hymn is built on taking refuge in her. There is nowhere for her to go.

Niravadyā rewards etymology. Avadya is formed from the root vad, to speak, with the negative prefix and the gerundive ending: literally what is not to be said. What is not to be said is what is disgraceful, and so avadya comes to mean fault or blemish. Blamelessness in Sanskrit is a fact about speech before it is a fact about conduct — there is nothing to be said against her, and so nothing to be said.

Nirantarā closes the verse and the word is in ordinary use for anything continuous or incessant. Antara is an interval, a gap, and also the inside of a thing and a difference between two things; all three senses are live. Without gaps, without an inside distinct from an outside, without difference. The tradition reads it as the denial of the three kinds of distinction that Advaita enumerates — the difference of a thing from another of its own kind, from a thing of another kind, and from its own parts — which is exactly the ground the hymn will cover again at nirbhedā four verses from now.
commentary.practice:
Every one of the eight names in this verse is four syllables long, and no other verse in the hymn is built so squarely. Nit-ya-muk-tā, nir-vi-kā-rā, niṣ-pra-pañ-cā, ni-rā-śra-yā, nit-ya-śud-dhā, nit-ya-bud-dhā, ni-ra-vad-yā, ni-ran-ta-rā. Count them out once and then let the metre carry you; the danger in this verse is not stumbling but drifting, because nothing in the rhythm ever changes.

Niṣprapañcā holds the hardest cluster in the batch: retroflex ṣ, then p, then r, three consonants with no vowel among them, at the start of the second syllable. Break it as niṣ-pra-pañ-cā and rebuild slowly. The ñ later in the same word is the palatal nasal, made at the same place as the c that follows it, so the tongue does not move between them — the sequence ñca requires one gesture, not two.

The two nitya names in the second line differ by a single consonant and are otherwise identical: nityaśuddhā and nityabuddhā. Both contain the doubled voiced aspirate ddh, which means holding the d closed for a full beat and then releasing it with breath — śud-dhā, bud-dhā. Most reciters shorten one or the other; the metre wants both long. Chant the pair as a unit until the only thing that changes is ś against b.

Nitya itself is two syllables, nit-ya, with the t closing the first syllable. Do not let a vowel creep in. The three occurrences of nitya are the spine of the verse and they must all sound the same.

The rest of the clusters are milder and worth naming: rv in nirvikārā, dental r into the labiodental v; śr in nirāśrayā, palatal sibilant into r; dy in niravadyā; nt in nirantarā. Nirāśrayā and niravadyā also give a useful contrast in vowel weight — the first has a long ā in its second syllable and the second has a short a, and the metre will tell you at once if you get them the wrong way round.

There is no sandhi to unpick anywhere in this verse. Every name stands separate, and this is one of the very few places in the stotra where the written line can be read off exactly as it is heard. If the Devanagari of the long compounds has been giving trouble, this is a good verse to read aloud from the script rather than from the transliteration.

The caesura is after nirāśrayā, and there is no reason to breathe anywhere else.

For contemplation, the three nitya names are the instruction. Each of them removes a beginning. It is easy to hear forever free as a compliment paid to somebody else; the tradition's use of the verse is to turn it around, since the point of asserting that freedom was never absent is to raise the question of who exactly is supposed to be acquiring it. This is the verse in the batch most often quoted on its own in Advaitic settings, and it is the one that best repays being chanted slowly enough to hear as eight separate statements rather than as a single wash of negation.

046.subtitle: Without a cause, without a master

commentary.meaning: The first half of this verse contains the two most radical names in the whole negative series. Niṣkāraṇā says that nothing produced her, which cuts the chain of causes rather than extending it. Nirīśvarā says that there is no lord over her — and the word it uses, īśvara, is the ordinary Sanskrit word for God, so that a hymn to a goddess has here called her godless in the strict sense: there is nobody above. Between them sit two more removals, one about the moon's dark patch and one about the limiting adjuncts by which anything is narrowed down to being this rather than that. Then the second line changes the shape of the verse and of the four that follow it. Instead of eight removals it gives two pairs, and each pair puts a thing she is free of beside the same thing she destroys. She is untouched by passion and she grinds passion away; no rush of pride reaches her and she ends the drunkenness of self-regard in others. The negations have stopped being about her alone.
commentary.history:
Niṣkāraṇā is the point at which the hymn takes the argument from effects back to its end and refuses to go further. Sanskrit philosophy is unusually fond of the regress: everything has a cause, and the question is whether the series stops. The Śvetāśvatara's answer is the one this name assumes — that there is no lord over him in the world, no ruler, not even a sign by which he might be recognised; that he is the cause, and the master of the masters of the sense-faculties; that nobody begot him and nobody is set above him. Two of the names in this verse are in that single stanza. Nirīśvarā takes the first half of it and niṣkāraṇā the second.

Nirīśvarā deserves its shock. The word nirīśvara is the standard label in Indian doxography for a system that does without a god: classical Sāṃkhya is called nirīśvara-sāṃkhya precisely in contrast to the theistic kind. Applied to Lalitā the word means something different — no one holds authority over her — but the tradition has always felt the edge on it, and the edge is sharpened by where the name sits. Twenty-four names ago she was Śambhu's own, Śarva's wife, Śaṅkara's. Forty-seven names from now she will be sarveśvarī, sovereign of all. Here, between the two, she has no lord at all. A hymn that spends its first hundred names on her husband's arms and its later names on her sovereignty puts in the middle of the sequence a name that says the chain of authority simply ends.

Nirupādhi brings in the central working term of Advaita. An upādhi is a limiting adjunct: Monier-Williams gives it as a substitute, a disguise, something that has the mere name or appearance of another thing. The standard illustrations are the red flower that makes a colourless crystal look red and the pot that seems to enclose a piece of space. In each case something unlimited is made to look limited by an accident of proximity, and the whole apparatus of individual selfhood is analysed that way. To call her nirupādhiḥ is to say that every predicate in this hymn, including the ones being recited at that moment, is a flower held up beside a crystal. The stotra returns to the word much later, at name seven hundred and eight, where she is called wholly released from all limiting adjuncts.

Niṣkalaṅkā looks like a repetition of niṣkalā from the previous verse and is not related to it at all. Kalaṅka is a stain or a blot, and its most familiar use is for the dark mark on the moon; kalā, a part or a digit, is a different word that merely sounds similar. Placed two verses apart the two names make a small trap for the reader and a small joke for the listener.

The second line begins a pattern that will run for four verses. From here to name one hundred and eighty-one the hymn works in couples: a name saying she is free of some affliction, immediately followed by a name saying she destroys it. Nīrāgā and rāgamathanī, nirmadā and madanāśinī, and then in the next verses the same shape applied to delusion, possessiveness, sin, anger, greed, doubt, worldly existence, division and death. What the pairing asserts is that her freedom is not a private condition. She is not merely clean; she is corrosive.

Rāga returning here is the most pointed thing in the verse. At the eighth name of this hymn, in its second verse, the noose in her hand was declared to be the very form of rāga — not a symbol of desire but desire itself, held as her own equipment. A hundred and fifty names later she is free of rāga and grinds it away. The tradition does not treat this as a contradiction and does not try to explain it away. The position, stated as plainly as it can be, is that the force which binds and the force which releases are one power differently directed, and that the rope is being held at the other end. A reader who has kept the second verse in mind will hear this pair as its completion rather than its retraction.

Mada is the last word here and it is a wonderfully physical one. Monier-Williams gives it as intoxication, rapture, rut — including specifically the rut of an elephant and the fluid that runs from its temples — and then, by an entirely natural extension, as pride. The name says that this heat never rises in her. There is also an accident of spelling worth registering without making too much of it: the letters of madanāśinī contain madana, which is Kāma, the god of desire whom Śiva burnt to ash, from whose ashes Bhaṇḍāsura was made, and whom she afterwards restored to life. The name means destroyer of intoxication. The language leaves the other reading lying about, in a hymn that has been circling Kāma since its second verse.
commentary.practice:
The prefix takes three different shapes in the first four names of this verse and the change is the main thing to hear. Niṣkāraṇā and niṣkalaṅkā have the retroflex ṣ before k. Nirupādhiḥ has r before a vowel. And then nīrāgā, at the head of the second line, has no consonant from the prefix at all: before an r the s of nis simply disappears and the i is lengthened in compensation, giving nī-rā-gā with a long first syllable. Two names later nirmadā restores the r. The four forms are within eight seconds of each other and a reciter who hears them as four different words has misunderstood the verse.

The retroflex ṇ of niṣkāraṇā belongs to kāraṇa and is not produced by the prefix; the same ṇ appears in every derivative of that root. Niṣkalaṅkā has the guttural nasal ṅ before k, made at the back of the mouth in the same place as the k, so nothing moves between them: niṣ-ka-laṅ-kā, with the ṅk cluster as one gesture.

The join between the third and fourth names is written into the script and worth pausing on. Nirupādhiḥ ends in a visarga; the next name begins with the voiced n of nirīśvarā; so the visarga becomes r and the two names are printed as one word, निरुपाधिर्निरीश्वरा. This is the same rule that produced bhadramūrtir bhakta- five verses ago and will produce mahālakṣmīr and mahābuddhir later in this batch. When the verse is chanted, the r is heard and the word boundary is not — which is exactly why the name is nirupādhiḥ and not nirupādhir when it is offered on its own.

Nirīśvarā packs three long vowels and the cluster śv into four syllables: ni-rīś-va-rā. The ś is the palatal sibilant and the v is made with the lower lip against the upper teeth. Both are commonly lost. Say the whole word slowly and make sure the ī of the second syllable is genuinely long, because a short i turns the name into nothing at all.

Mathanī has an aspirated dental th — tongue-tip at the teeth, released with a puff — and it is never the th of English thing, a sound Sanskrit does not have. The root is manth, to churn, the same verb used of the churning of the ocean and of Śiva as the churner of the three cities. Hearing the th properly is the difference between crushing passion and merely mentioning it.

The two pairs in the second line are built on echoes and the echoes should be audible. Nīrāgā rāgamathanī puts rāga at the end of one name and the start of the next; nirmadā madanāśinī does the same with mada. Chant each pair as a single arc with the shared word at the join, and the second line stops being four names and becomes two statements.

Metrically the first line is four names of four syllables and the second is three plus five, twice. Breathe after nirīśvarā, at the halfway point, which is also where the verse changes its argument.

For what to hold: this is the verse in the batch that most rewards being read against the beginning of the hymn. Keep the second verse in mind — the noose in her hand that was said to be desire's own form — and then chant nīrāgā rāgamathanī. The tradition's counsel at this point is not to treat the two as stages, as though she had once been attached and had got over it, but as one description from two sides.

commentary.meaning: Two solitary names and then three matched pairs, and the whole verse is about the first person. Nothing worries her, because there is no outcome she has to secure. The habit of saying I has no purchase in her — and ahaṃkāra is not vanity but a technical term, the faculty that claims an experience as somebody's. Then the pairs: free of delusion and the destroyer of delusion, without a sense of mine and the killer of possessiveness, sinless and the destroyer of sin. Each pair says the same thing twice, once about her and once about what she does to whoever comes near. The order within each pair is not arbitrary. She can burn the fog off because she was never in it. What is striking is which two things the verse chooses to abolish between delusion and sin: the word I and the word mine. They are the two smallest words in the language and the hymn treats them as the whole disease.
commentary.history:
Ahaṃkāra needs its Sāṃkhya setting or the name will be read as a moral compliment. In that system the world unfolds from an unconscious ground through a series of principles, and the third of them is ahaṃkāra, defined in a single word: abhimāna, the act of taking something as one's own. From it two lines of evolution branch, the eleven faculties on one side and the five subtle elements on the other, so that everything a person is equipped with and everything a person perceives are alike products of the I-maker. It is a piece of machinery, not a character flaw. The upaniṣads had already told a story about how it arose. In the oldest of them, the self alone was there in the beginning, in the shape of a person; it looked around, saw nothing but itself, and said I am — and from that the word I came to exist. Nirahaṅkārā denies the whole apparatus at its root.

Nirmamā and mamatāhantrī take the other half. Mama is the genitive of the first person pronoun, simply mine; mamatā is that word made into an abstract noun, mineness. Sanskrit does this readily and the result is a word for the state of regarding things as belonging to one. The Bhagavad Gītā pairs the two terms in exactly the way this verse does, more than once: the man who has given up all desires and moves without longing, without mine and without I, comes to peace. Śānti is where the Gītā's sentence lands, and śāntā was a name in this hymn six names before nirahaṅkārā. The stotra is assembling its Gītā verse out of parts.

Niścintā opens the verse and it is the lightest of the eight in weight and the heaviest in ordinary usefulness. Cintā is anxious thought, the mind revolving something it cannot settle. It is worth noticing that the same word stands inside cintāmaṇi, the wish-granting stone, which is what her palace is built of in the standard visualisation — the gem that yields whatever is thought of. In one word thought is the disease and in the other it is the currency of the granted wish. The hymn has already put her inside the cintāmaṇi house by implication; here it says there is no cintā in her.

The three destroyer-names deserve a word about what they are for. It is of no practical use to a reciter that the goddess personally has no delusion, no possessiveness and no sin; a hymn made only of such statements would be a description of somebody enviable and nothing more. Every one of these pairs therefore turns outward on its second half. The doctrinal claim being made by the pairing, rather than by either name alone, is that she can remove these things from a devotee precisely because they are not in her — the tradition's standing objection to seeking help from any power that is itself entangled. This is why the negative names and the destroyer-names are always in that order and never the reverse.

Pāpanāśinī is also a promise the text makes about itself. The phalaśruti appended to this stotra claims among other things that reciting the thousand names destroys accumulated wrongdoing, and the hymn will come back to the subject with a much bigger word at name two hundred and fourteen, mahāpātakanāśinī, the destroyer of the great sins — the specific and enumerated crimes of the law books, for which ordinary expiation was held not to suffice. Here the word is the ordinary one. What is being offered at this point in the hymn is not yet the extraordinary remedy but the everyday one.
commentary.practice:
The rhythm of this verse is exact and worth internalising before anything else: three syllables then five, four times over. Niś-cin-tā, ni-ra-haṅ-kā-rā. Nir-mo-hā, mo-ha-nā-śi-nī. Nir-ma-mā, ma-ma-tā-han-trī. Niṣ-pā-pā, pā-pa-nā-śi-nī. Four quarters, all built the same way. If the count is right the verse almost recites itself.

Niścintā gives the prefix another face. Before the palatal c of cintā, the s of nis becomes the palatal sibilant ś: niś-cin-tā. That is now the fifth shape of the same prefix in five verses, and the reason is simple assimilation — the sibilant takes the place of articulation of the consonant it is about to meet. Compare niṣ- before k in niṣpāpā's neighbours and nis- before t in nistulā three verses from now, where the sibilant stays dental because t is dental.

Nirahaṅkārā has the guttural nasal ṅ, made at the back of the mouth where the k is made. Do not substitute the n of English sing-along by moving the tongue forward. Say ni-ra-haṅ-kā-rā with the ṅ and the k as one gesture at the velum, and let the h before it be a full breathy sound rather than a swallowed one.

Mamatāhantrī holds the hardest cluster: ntr, dental nasal, dental stop and r in succession, with no vowel among them. Break it as ma-ma-tā-han-trī. The trī at the end is the feminine agent suffix that also gave dāyinī its counterparts elsewhere in the hymn, and it is always long.

The three pairs are joined by repeated words and the repetition should be heard rather than smoothed away. Nirmohā mohanāśinī puts moha at the end of one name and the start of the next; nirmamā mamatāhantrī repeats mama; niṣpāpā pāpanāśinī repeats pāpa. This is a recognised figure in Sanskrit poetics, and the effect is of a word being handed across a gap. Chant each pair as one arc and let the joint be audible.

Watch the vowel lengths in the third pair. Niṣpāpā has three long syllables in a row, niṣ-pā-pā, and pāpanāśinī begins long and then goes short: pā-pa-nā-śi-nī. Reciters who have got into a rhythm will tend to lengthen the second a of pāpanāśinī and the metre will collapse.

One clean contrast in the sibilants: the ś of niścintā and of the three -nāśinī endings is palatal, while the ṣ of niṣpāpā is retroflex. Both appear in the same verse and neither is the s of English.

The breath goes after mohanāśinī. In the archanā form the verse gives eight salutations, and the pairs are usually offered without a pause between them.

For what to hold: the two names in the middle are the instruction, and they are unusually concrete for this stretch of the hymn. Not a doctrine about the self, but two words — I and mine — presented as the things to be given up. The traditional counsel is to notice, while chanting, how often either word has been used in the last hour, and to let the pair that follows do its work on that rather than on anything abstract.

commentary.meaning: The most symmetrical verse in the hymn. Four pairs, one to a quarter, each pair naming a thing she is free of and then the same thing she destroys: anger, greed, doubt and bhava, which here means the whole business of coming into existence and going out of it again. The first three are ordinary afflictions and the fourth is not; putting them in one line says that being born is an affliction of the same order as losing one's temper, and can be dealt with the same way. Doubt is the strange one to find in this company. Anger and greed are appetites and their cure is obvious in kind, but a doubt is a question, and a hymn that promises to kill doubt rather than answer it is making a claim about what recitation is for. The verse ends where the reciter's interest ends, with the round of becoming brought to a close for anyone who asks it of her.
commentary.history:
Look back over the last five verses and a list emerges. The traditional enumeration of the enemies within is six: kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada and mātsarya — wanting, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication and envy. Since the beginning of the negative series the hymn has removed five of them by name, in this order: niṣkāmā at a hundred and forty-two, nirmadā at a hundred and fifty-eight, nirmohā at a hundred and sixty-two, and now niṣkrodhā and nirlobhā. It has also added rāga, passion, which is not on the standard list but is on the Yoga Sūtra's list of afflictions. Only one of the six is missing, and it is mātsarya, envy — and the word does not occur anywhere in the thousand names. Whether that is deliberate or simply the result of composing under an alliterative constraint is not knowable, but the omission is complete.

Anger returning here has the same force that passion had two verses ago. In the second verse of this hymn the goad in her hand was said to have the shape of krodha: not a weapon against anger but a weapon made of it. Now she is free of anger and quells it in others. Both of the objects she was described as holding at the beginning of the stotra have now been taken back and turned into things she abolishes, and neither statement is withdrawn.

Saṃśaya is the interesting member of the set because it belongs to a different order of trouble. In Indian philosophy doubt is a technical category — one of the standing obstacles to knowledge, the state in which two alternatives are entertained and neither settles — and the Gītā is unusually harsh about it, saying that the man of doubt has neither this world nor the next nor any happiness at all, and instructing Arjuna to cut doubt with the sword of knowledge rather than to resolve it item by item. Saṃśayaghnī does exactly that: the suffix ghnī is from the root han, to strike, and it makes her a killer of doubt rather than an answerer of questions.

The most important passage behind this pair is in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, where the knot of the heart is split, all doubts are cut and one's works are exhausted, all at the moment of seeing. That verse matters for this hymn twice over. It supplies the language of cutting doubt, and it supplies the knot: at names one hundred, one hundred and two and one hundred and four, only nine verses back, Lalitā was called the splitter of the knot of Brahmā, the knot of Viṣṇu and the knot of Rudra as she rose through the cakras. The three knots are the tradition's expansion of the Muṇḍaka's single hṛdayagranthi. The stotra used the image then and now uses the sequel.

Nirbhavā and bhavanāśinī close the verse and close a circle. This batch of verses opened seven verses ago with bhavānī, wife of Bhava, and then bhavāraṇyakuṭhārikā, the axe to the forest of bhava, where the same syllable was made to mean the god and the world in consecutive names. Here, sixty names later, the negative series collides with the same word from a third direction: she does not come into being at all, and she brings coming-into-being to an end. Three treatments of bhava within one batch, each in a different register, and the alliterative machinery that governs this whole section is what brought them together.
commentary.practice:
The verse is built out of four pairs and the pairs are not all the same length, which is where reciters trip. The first, second and fourth quarters run three plus five — niṣ-kro-dhā, kro-dha-śa-ma-nī; nir-lo-bhā, lo-bha-nā-śi-nī; nir-bha-vā, bha-va-nā-śi-nī. The third quarter is four plus four: niḥ-saṃ-śa-yā, saṃ-śa-ya-ghnī. That one asymmetry in the middle of an otherwise mechanical verse is worth marking deliberately, because a reciter running on the three-plus-five rhythm will arrive at saṃśayaghnī a syllable early.

Niṣkrodhā opens with three consonants in a row across a syllable boundary: retroflex ṣ, then k, then r. Say niṣ as a closed syllable with the tongue-tip curled back, then release into kro with the r fully tapped. The same krodha then begins the next name unencumbered, which makes the pair a useful before-and-after drill for the cluster.

Niḥsaṃśayā is the last of the prefix's shapes and the plainest: before a sibilant the s of nis stays a visarga, a light voiceless breath. Say niḥ with a faint echo of the vowel after it — nihi, very short — and then saṃ. Do not turn it into nis or nish. Across these seven verses the same prefix has now appeared as nir, niṣ, niś, nis, nī and niḥ, and this is the last of them.

Saṃśayaghnī contains two things worth slowing for. The anusvāra before ś is a nasalisation coloured by the sibilant that follows, not a full n. And ghnī is a voiced aspirated guttural followed immediately by a dental n: gh-nī, with the breath released on the gh before the tongue moves forward for the n. It is one of the rarer clusters in the language and most reciters simplify it to a plain g.

The aspirates carry this verse generally. Krodhā has dh, lobhā and bhavā have bh, ghnī has gh, and every one of them must be heard as a stop released with breath. In a verse this repetitive the aspiration is the first thing to go.

One length to guard: nirlobhā has a long o, and lobhanāśinī keeps it long in the first syllable and then goes short. Lo-bha-nā-śi-nī. The same pattern holds in bhavanāśinī, where the first two syllables are both short.

The breath goes after lobhanāśinī, at the end of the first line.

For contemplation, the third pair is the one to sit with, because it is the odd one out. Anger and greed are things one would obviously like to be rid of; doubt is a state most educated people rather respect. The hymn puts it between greed and death and treats it as the same kind of thing. Whether that is right is itself a question the verse is not proposing to answer, which is roughly the point. The traditional use of this verse is straightforward: it is among the passages recited by people who want something specific stopped, and the second name of each pair is what they are asking for.

049.subtitle: No division, no death, no act

commentary.meaning: Eight more names and the negations are now cutting close to the bone. She admits no mental construction: nothing is sorted, compared or set against an alternative in her, which places her where a good deal of Indian thought locates the goal, at the point where the mind stops making distinctions. Nothing presses on her, and there is no seam anywhere along which one part of her could be told from another — followed at once by the destroyer of division, which is the most consequential of all the destroyer-names in the batch, since the division most in need of destroying is the one between the person reciting and the person recited to. Then imperishable and the crusher of death, which is what the worshipper actually wants. Then the last two, and they are quietly extreme. She does nothing at all. She takes nothing in and keeps nothing back — no property, no household, no retinue, said of a goddess whose entire cult consists of offerings made to her in the middle of nine enclosures of attendants.
commentary.history:
Nirvikalpā is a word with three careers. In the analysis of perception it names the first bare instant of seeing, before the thing seen has been sorted under a name; in Yoga it is the higher of the two kinds of absorption, the one in which no object, word or idea remains; and in ritual grammar a vikalpa is simply an option, a place where the rules allow a choice. Patañjali defines vikalpa tightly: an idea that follows on words and has no object behind it. To call her nirvikalpā is to say that she is not one of the things a mind arrives at by talking to itself, and it is the closest this hymn comes to admitting that its own thousand words are in a difficult position.

Nirbhedā and bhedanāśinī are the doctrinal centre of the verse. Advaita analyses difference into three kinds: the difference between a thing and its own parts, between a thing and another of the same class, and between a thing and something of an entirely different class. A tree differs from its branches in the first way, from another tree in the second, and from a stone in the third. To be nirbheda is to have none of the three, which is the technical definition of the absolute. The upaniṣadic version of the claim is blunter and is the sentence this verse is standing on: there is no plurality here at all, and whoever sees as if there were goes from death to death. That sentence is doing double duty, because it also supplies the verse's next pair. In the upaniṣad the penalty for seeing division is death, and here the destroyer of division is followed immediately by the crusher of death.

Mṛtyumathanī is what a great many people who recite this hymn are actually asking for, and the tradition has never pretended otherwise. The oldest prayer in the language on this subject is the tryambaka verse of the Ṛgveda, which asks to be released from death as a cucumber is released from its stalk, and which is recited in South India to this day for the sick and the dying. The verb in the name is worth noticing: manth or math, to churn, to grind by turning — the same root that produced the epithet of Śiva as the churner of the three cities, which Śaṅkara uses of him in the Saundaryalaharī. Death here is not defeated in single combat. It is worn away by rotation.

Niṣkriyā puts the paradox of this whole section at its sharpest. The hymn began with a war. She rose from the fire to kill Bhaṇḍāsura, she burnt his city of Śūnyaka to nothing with the Kāmeśvara weapon, and eighty names ago the stotra described the battle in detail. Now she does not act. The Śvetāśvatara had already put the two together, calling the one controller of the many inactive ones, and the tradition's reading is that action is a category that applies to what is inside the world and she is not. It is the same manoeuvre that Vedānta makes about brahman as the cause of everything and the doer of nothing.

Niṣparigrahā is the last name and it is stranger than it looks. Parigraha means a taking hold of on all sides, and it runs from acceptance of a gift, through property, to a household, a retinue, and a wife. As aparigraha it is one of the five restraints binding a yogin in Patañjali's list, and there it means not accumulating. Said of Lalitā it is startling in three directions at once. She is worshipped with offerings, and accepts nothing. She is enthroned in the middle of a Śrīcakra whose nine enclosures are populated entirely by attendant goddesses, and she has no retinue. And she has been called the wife of Bhava, Śarva and Śaṅkara in this very batch, and here she belongs to no household. The negative series, which began by removing a support and a stain, ends by removing her possessions, her staff and her marriage.
commentary.practice:
The rhythm of this verse alternates rather than repeating, and knowing the pattern is the whole trick. The first quarter is four plus four, nir-vi-kal-pā and ni-rā-bā-dhā. Then three quarters of three plus five: nir-bhe-dā, bhe-da-nā-śi-nī; nir-nā-śā, mṛ-tyu-ma-tha-nī; niṣ-kri-yā, niṣ-pa-ri-gra-hā. That last pair is the only one in the verse whose two names are not built out of the same word, which is why it feels like a stop.

Nirnāśā deserves attention because of what it does not do. Elsewhere in the hymn an r pulls a following n back to the retroflex position — that is why śarvāṇī has a ṇ where bhavānī has an n. Here the r of nir stands immediately before the n of nāśa and the text as transmitted keeps a dental n throughout: nir-nā-śā, two dental sounds in succession. Say it with the tongue-tip forward for both and do not let the r drag the n backwards out of habit. Listening for this is a good test of whether the retroflexes elsewhere in the verse are being made deliberately or by accident.

Mṛtyumathanī has the vocalic ṛ, which is a syllable in its own right: a short r sound with a faint vowel colour around it, made with the tongue-tip curled towards the roof of the mouth. It is not ri and it is not ru, though most reciters approximate one or the other according to where they were trained. Then tyu, a dental t with y. Then tha, the aspirated dental — again not the th of English. The whole word is five syllables and the only long one is the last.

Niṣkriyā stacks retroflex ṣ, k and r before the vowel: niṣ-kri-yā. Niṣparigrahā stacks ṣ and p at the same place and then adds gr in the middle: niṣ-pa-ri-gra-hā. Both are easier if the closed syllable niṣ is finished cleanly before the next consonant begins.

Nirvikalpā has the cluster lp, and nirābādhā has an aspirated dh between two long ā vowels. Neither is hard, but nirābādhā is the only wholly open, unhurried word in the verse and it is worth letting it be one.

Bhedanāśinī repeats bheda from the name before it, and this is the last of the echoing pairs; from the next verse the hymn changes its prefix and its method. Give the join its full value one more time.

The breath goes after bhedanāśinī.

For what to hold: the second name of the second pair is the one the tradition points to. Bheda between worshipper and worshipped is the difference that a thousand names in the third person keep manufacturing, and the meditation verses at the head of this stotra had already dealt with it in three words, saying that one contemplates Bhavānī as simply I. Chanting bhedanāśinī with that line in mind is the intended use of this name. The other thing to notice, if the verse is taken slowly, is the order of the last four: no perishing, death crushed, no action, nothing possessed. Having removed death, the hymn removes the two things a person spends a life doing.

050.subtitle: The end of the negations, and Durgā

commentary.meaning: The long negative run finishes in the first line of this verse and then the hymn changes prefix. Four last removals — nothing to weigh her against, nothing that departs from her, nothing that lapses — and among them, without warning, her hair. Nīlacikurā is a plain physical description dropped into the middle of metaphysics, the same intrusion that put her face and her waist into the verse where the negations began, and it is the one dark thing in a goddess who has been red since the meditation verses. Then dur- takes over from nir- and the grammar is identical while the sense is opposite: hard to obtain, hard to approach, and then, in two syllables, Durgā — the only place in the thousand names where that name appears. The verse closes with the first straightforwardly positive pair in fifty-six names. She strikes sorrow down, and having taken it away she does not leave the space empty.
commentary.history:
The negative series ends at niratyayā, the hundred and eighty-seventh name, having run without a break since nirādhārā. What follows is not a change of method but a change of material. The prefix dus behaves exactly as nis does: it becomes dur before a vowel or a voiced consonant, and it keeps a visarga before the unvoiced kh of duḥkha, which is precisely the pattern the reciter has spent seven verses learning. What has changed is the meaning. Nis subtracts; dus says that a thing is hard or bad. The hymn hands the same machine to a different word and produces the opposite kind of epithet, and the seam is at the end of the first line.

Nistulā is the best of the last four. Tulā is a balance, the pair of scales, and it is also the word for the ordeal by weighing in the law books, in which an accused person is placed in one pan and matched against a counterweight. From that comes the whole vocabulary of comparison: to be equal to something is to be in the balance with it. The stotra has spent forty verses comparing her to things, and much of the classical poetry that stands behind it — the Saundaryalaharī's weighing of her lips against coral and the bimba fruit, for instance — is built on the figure of the failed comparison. Nistulā says that there is nothing to put in the other pan.

Then the hair. This is the third time a body has broken into an abstract passage in this batch, after the autumn-moon face and the slender waist seven verses back, and it is the most conspicuous because of the colour. Nīla is the blue-black of the rain cloud and of the blue lotus, and in a hymn where she has been red from the first meditation verse — vermilion, dawn-coloured, a flood of red light drowning the world-eggs — her hair is the single dark thing about her. The Saundaryalaharī compares that mass of hair to a grove of blue lotuses and then claims that heaven's flowers move into it for the sake of its natural scent, which is the fullest treatment the tradition gives the image.

Durgā is the event of this verse. Of the thousand names, this is the only one that is simply the name of another goddess in her own right and nothing more, and it goes past in two syllables. Its oldest sense is not a person at all. In the Veda durga is a hard place: a defile, a difficult crossing, a stronghold. The hymn of the Durgā Sūkta asks Agni to carry us over all difficult places as a boat carries one over a river, and the Kaṭha Upaniṣad calls the path to the self a razor's edge, hard to cross, and says that the wise call that path a durga. Both of those senses sit inside the names on either side. Durlabhā, hard to get, and durgamā, hard to approach, are not describing an obstacle standing in front of her; they are saying that the difficulty is what she is. And durga as fortress gives the name its other classical reading, the stronghold that cannot be stormed.

What the name also does is import a whole other goddess and her literature. Durgā of the Devī Māhātmya is the warrior who kills Mahiṣa and Śumbha, and the great hymns of that text are addressed to her by name; one of the best known asks who but she, remembered, takes away the fear of every living creature, and calls her the remover of poverty, sorrow and fear. Two of those three appear here. Duḥkhahantrī is the next name but one, and bhayāpahā was a name eight verses back. The Lalitā tradition and the Devī Māhātmya tradition are distinct — different texts, different rites, different lineages — and this is one of the places where the later hymn reaches over and takes what it needs.

Duḥkhahantrī and sukhapradā close the verse and turn the hymn round. For fifty-six names the method has been removal; the last pair removes something and then puts something in its place. It is the hinge into the verses that follow, where every name will begin with sarva, all.
commentary.practice:
Two prefixes, one grammar. In the first line nis appears as nis before the dental t of nistulā, as nī with a long vowel and no consonant before the r of nīrāgā's cousin — here nī-la, though that nī is part of the word for blue and not the prefix at all, which is exactly the trap — and as nir before the vowels of nirapāyā and niratyayā. In the second line dus appears as dur before the voiced l and g of durlabhā, durgamā and durgā, and as duḥ before the unvoiced kh of duḥkhahantrī. Learning that these are two words behaving identically, rather than four or five separate forms, is the single most useful thing this verse teaches.

Nīlacikurā is where reciters go wrong, because after seven verses of ni- prefixes the ear expects another one. It is not. The word is nīla, blue-black, with a long ī, and then cikura, hair. Four short syllables follow the long one: nī-la-ci-ku-rā. Get the length of that first syllable right and the metre holds; treat it as a negative prefix and the whole quarter collapses.

Duḥkha has to be given its visarga. It is duḥ, with a light voiceless breath echoing the u, and then kha, an aspirated guttural. It is not dukkha, which is the Pali form and which most English speakers have met first, and it is not duka. The h of the visarga and the h of the aspiration are two separate events. Say duḥ-kha-han-trī slowly; there are three h sounds in the word and each is doing a different job.

The cluster ntr in hantrī is the same one that appeared in mamatāhantrī three verses ago, and the same feminine agent ending. Sukhapradā, by contrast, is four completely open syllables and is the easiest word in the batch — which is appropriate, since it is the only name in fifty-six that gives something outright.

Durgā is two syllables and both are heavy: dur with a full r, gā long. It is the shortest name in this batch and it should not be hurried through on the way to the next one. In practice many reciters mark it, slightly, and there is a reason to.

The metre is worth noticing because the third quarter repeats a rhythm from earlier in the batch exactly. Durlabhā durgamā durgā is three plus three plus two, which is the shape of nirlepā nirmalā nityā six verses back. The first quarter is three plus five, the second and fourth are four plus four. Breathe after niratyayā, which is also where the negations stop.

For contemplation this verse offers a change of posture. Fifty-six names have been removals, and it is possible to chant them and end up somewhere rather cold. The last two names of this verse are the tradition's own correction. Sorrow is struck down, which is a violent word, and then something is handed over. The traditional use of the verse follows the same logic: this is the passage people recite for someone who is suffering, and the name they are reciting toward is the last one.
