references.note: Listen for the shift at the middle of the verse, where nir- gives way to dur-. It is audible in a good recitation, and it is the end of the longest single pattern in the hymn.

commentary.meaning: Three names in dur- and do-, then three in sa-, and the verse turns on the join. The first three are about distance and defect: she keeps far from the corrupt, she quiets bad conduct, and no flaw has been left in her. Then, without transition, she knows everything, her compassion comes dense, and there is no one level with her or above her. The two halves look like they belong to different hymns, and the tension between them is real. A goddess who is far from the wicked is not obviously the same goddess whose pity is described as thick rather than thinly spread. The tradition's answer is in the second name of the verse: what she does with bad conduct is quieten it, not punish it, so that the distance is something the corrupt experience rather than something she maintains. The last name is the largest claim in the verse and the most compressed. It denies at once that anyone is her equal and that anyone is her superior, which is what a Sanskrit text says when it means to place something at the top.
commentary.history:
The last name of the verse is a quotation, compressed to eight syllables. The Śvetāśvatara says of the supreme that no action and no instrument of action can be found in him, and that no one equal to him or greater than him is seen. Samānādhikavarjitā takes the second half of that line and turns it into a name. The rest of the stanza matters just as much, because it continues by saying that his highest power is heard of as manifold, and that it is natural to him, consisting of knowledge, strength and action. That sentence is the oldest and most quoted upaniṣadic use of the word śakti, and the tradition that made a goddess of śakti has always treated it as its charter. It is also, as it happens, the seed of the next four verses of this hymn: sarvaśaktimayī comes at the start of the next verse, and knowledge, strength and action arrive as mahābuddhiḥ, mahābalā and mahāvīryā in the last verse of this batch.

Sarvajñā is the only occurrence of that name in the thousand, which is surprising for so obvious an epithet. The word is old and precise. The Muṇḍaka says that from the one who knows everything and is aware of everything, whose austerity consists of knowledge, come forth this brahman, name, form and food — knowing there is productive rather than merely comprehensive. And Śaṅkara's opening sentence in the Brahmasūtra commentary, from which this batch has already drawn three names, ends with exactly these two words: all-knowing, and furnished with every power. Sarvajñā here and sarvaśaktimayī in the next verse complete the borrowing.

Duṣṭadūrā is the name that gives commentators trouble and it deserves to. A goddess who keeps her distance from the wicked is not the goddess of the phalaśruti, which promises that reciting these names destroys the sins of anyone who recites them, nor of pāpanāśinī four verses back. Two readings are available and both are old. On the first, the distance is not hers: she is equally present everywhere, and the corrupt are the ones who fail to find her however close they stand, which is what the word dūra, far, means when it is used of something omnipresent. On the second, dūra keeps its ordinary force and the name is a warning rather than a description of her nature. The next name settles which reading the verse intends. Durācāraśamanī uses śamana, the causing of quiet — the same word that produced krodhaśamanī three verses ago — and not any of the many available words for punishment. Bad conduct is put to sleep rather than answered.

The contrast with the Bhagavad Gītā is worth making because the Gītā's line is so familiar. There the descent of the divine into the world has three purposes: to rescue the good, to destroy the wrongdoers, and to establish dharma. Vināśāya duṣkṛtām — the wrongdoers, not the wrongdoing. The sahasranāma, in a verse using the same root as duṣkṛt, declines the second purpose. It quiets durācāra and keeps its distance from the duṣṭa, and it never says that she destroys anybody except demons.

Sāndrakaruṇā is the name that makes the verse. Sāndra is a physical word before it is anything else: Monier-Williams gives viscid, unctuous, thick, solid, dense, and then intense. It is used of forests, of clouds, of ointment. Compassion described with that adjective is compassion that has body — poured rather than sprinkled, and continuous rather than occasional. The Devī Māhātmya reaches for the same idea with a different image when it asks who else has a heart that is always wet. Placed immediately after sarvajñā, the name also makes a claim about the relation of the two: she knows everything about you, and the compassion is not in spite of that.
commentary.practice:
This verse breaks a name across the caesura, which happens rarely and is worth knowing in advance. The first line is duṣṭadūrā, four syllables, then durācāraśamanī, seven, then doṣavarjitā, five. Four and seven make eleven, so the quarter boundary at the eighth syllable falls inside the second name, between durācāra and śamanī. Reciters do not break there. Take the whole first line in one arc and breathe at the end of it.

Duṣṭadūrā puts two retroflexes side by side at the start: ṣ then ṭ, tongue-tip curled back for both with no forward movement between them. Then the ordinary dental d of dūrā. Duṣ-ṭa-dū-rā. The contrast between the retroflex ṭ in the first half of the word and the dental d in the second is the whole pronunciation lesson, and it is a lesson that will be needed again immediately, because the next line is full of dental sibilants.

The second line is a study in s against ś and ṣ. Sarvajñā, sāndrakaruṇā and samānādhikavarjitā all open with the plain dental s, tongue-tip forward. There is no palatal ś anywhere in the line — the only other sibilant is the ṣ inside duṣṭa in the line above and the ś in śamanī. After seven verses in which almost every name opened with a retroflex ṣ or a palatal ś, the ear has to be reset.

Sarvajñā carries the cluster jñ, which is the same one that appeared in the very first verse of the stotra in mahārājñī. The value the grammarians describe is a palatal j followed by the palatal nasal ñ, both made with the tongue-body flat against the hard palate. Northern reciters will say something close to gy and southern reciters something close to jñ; the letter is jñ. Say sar-va-jñā with the tongue in one position for the whole cluster.

Sāndrakaruṇā holds three difficulties in five syllables. The cluster ndr is a dental nasal, a dental stop and an r with no vowel among them: sān-dra. The ṇ of karuṇā is retroflex, pulled back by the r earlier in the word, exactly as in kāraṇa and guṇa in the earlier verses. And the word begins long and ends long with three short syllables between, sān-dra-ka-ru-ṇā, so the rhythm must not sag in the middle.

Samānādhikavarjitā is eight syllables and fills the last quarter by itself. The join in the middle is a sandhi: samāna plus adhika, equal and greater, with the two a vowels merged into a single long ā. In the Devanagari it shows as one stroke and the eye has to reconstruct it. Say sa-mā-nā-dhi-ka-var-ji-tā and know that the fourth syllable is doing the work of two words.

For what to hold while chanting: the verse asks to be taken as one movement rather than two. It is easy to chant the first line as severity and the second as sweetness. The tradition reads them together, and the reading turns on the middle name — that what she does with wrongdoing is not to strike it but to settle it, which is also what she does with anger and doubt in the verses just past. Held that way, duṣṭadūrā stops sounding like a threat and starts sounding like a diagnosis.

commentary.meaning: Six names, and every one of them begins with sarva. After fifty-six names of subtraction the hymn has turned round and is now saying the same thing by addition, which is the shape of this entire stretch of the stotra: first nothing may be predicated of her, then everything must be. She is not described as possessing all powers but as being made of them, since the suffix maya means consisting of; wholly auspicious; the giver of the good road; sovereign of everything; made of everything; and, in the longest name of the verse, the very form of every mantra there is. That last name is the one the tradition treats as central, because it is not a compliment but a technical claim, and because it explains what the reciter is doing. If every mantra is her own body of sound, then the thousand names being spoken are not about her.
commentary.history:
It is worth stopping to see the architecture, because this verse is the far side of it. From nirādhārā to niratyayā the hymn removed fifty-six things. From sarvajñā in the last verse to the end of the mahā- block twenty verses further on, it adds. The two movements are the standard pair in Indian theology as in every other apophatic tradition, and they are not alternatives: the negative names deny that she is any particular thing, and the sarva names deny that she is other than any particular thing. Between them nothing is left over. The Chāndogya's formula for the same manoeuvre is three words long — all this is indeed brahman — and it is followed by the instruction to meditate on it in tranquillity.

Sarvaśaktimayī picks up where the last verse left off. The Śvetāśvatara stanza behind samānādhikavarjitā had continued by calling the supreme power manifold and natural to him, and this name completes the thought in the tradition's own vocabulary. The suffix is doing precise work. Maya, at the end of a compound, means made of: annamaya, made of food; ānandamaya, made of bliss. She does not wield the powers; she is their substance. In a system where śakti is a technical term for the active aspect of the absolute, saying that she is made of all śaktis is close to a definition.

Sarvamaṅgalā is the most publicly familiar name in the verse and the one with the widest life outside this text. Maṅgala is the auspicious in the widest sense, covering good omens, blessings, amulets, festivals and the customary opening prayer of any Sanskrit work. The most recited verse of the Devī Māhātmya addresses the goddess as the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, and that verse is said daily in more households than the whole of this stotra. When the Vāgdevatās put sarvamaṅgalā here they are naming her with a word already in every mouth.

Sarveśvarī is a reversal and the hymn means it as one. At name one hundred and fifty-five, forty-seven names ago, she was nirīśvarā, having no lord. Here she is the lord of all. The two names are not in different sections of a long text; they are within the same continuous movement, and they answer each other exactly. The Devī Māhātmya had already coined the superlative form when it said that the very goddess who is the cause of bondage in the world is the sovereign of all sovereigns, and this hymn will go one better at the end of the next batch with mahāyogeśvareśvarī.

Sadgatipradā is the quietest of the six and the most practical. Gati is a going, a course, and in the funerary vocabulary it is where the dead go; sadgati is the good destination, and the phrase is what one prays for on behalf of someone who has died. Sat also means real, so the compound can be heard as the going to what is. Placed among the great cosmic names, it is the one that a household would actually use.

Sarvamantrasvarūpiṇī needs its doctrine spelled out. In tantric thought the alphabet is not a notation but a substance. The fifty letters of Sanskrit are the mātṛkās, the little mothers, and in mātṛkānyāsa they are placed one by one on the body of the practitioner; the goddess is identified with the whole set. From that it follows directly that any mantra whatever, being made of those letters, is made of her — which is what this name says, and why it can say every mantra and not merely her own. Śrīvidyā has a narrower version of the same claim, that the fifteen-syllabled vidyā is the root of which other mantras are branches, and the frame narrative of this very stotra insists that the Śrīcakra, the mantra and the goddess are one thing under three descriptions. Two verses from now the hymn will state it more baldly still, calling her simply mahāmantrā, and the verse after that will add the yantra and the tantra. This name is where that sequence begins.
commentary.practice:
Six names beginning with the same two syllables, and the danger is a drone. The information is in what follows sarva, so give the second element of each compound its weight: -śaktimayī, -maṅgalā, -eśvarī, -mayī, -mantrasvarūpiṇī. The one name that does not begin with sarva, sadgatipradā, is in the middle of the first line and is the place to breathe mentally even though the metre does not stop there.

The first line is unusual in that both quarter boundaries fall inside names. Sarvaśaktimayī is six syllables, sarvamaṅgalā is five, sadgatipradā is five: six and five make eleven, so the eighth syllable lands in the middle of sarvamaṅgalā. As in the previous verse, do not break there. Take the line whole.

Sarveśvarī contains a sandhi that the Devanagari hides completely. The name is sarva plus īśvarī, and a final a meeting an initial ī gives a single e. What you see is सर्वेश्वरी and what is inside it is two words. The same fusion will produce mahāyogeśvareśvarī at the end of this batch, twice over in one word. Learning to see the e as a seam is one of the most useful habits a reader of this hymn can acquire.

Sadgatipradā hides a different one. The first element is sat, real or good, ending in an unvoiced dental t; before the voiced g of gati that t has been voiced to d. So sat plus gati gives sadgati, and the meaning of the name is only visible once the d is read back as a t. This is the same rule that turned cit into cid in cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā in the very first verse of the stotra.

Sarvamantrasvarūpiṇī is the mouthful and it has three separate difficulties. The cluster ntr, dental nasal into dental stop into r. Then sv, a dental sibilant into the labiodental v, immediately after it. Then the retroflex ṇ of -rūpiṇī, pulled back by the r earlier in the word. Break it as sar-va-man-tra-sva-rū-pi-ṇī, eight syllables filling the last quarter, and rebuild it slowly. The join between -mantra- and -sva- is where nearly everyone stumbles.

Two sibilant contrasts to keep clean. Sarvaśaktimayī has the dental s of sarva and then the palatal ś of śakti, two syllables apart. Sarvamantrasvarūpiṇī has three dental s sounds and no palatal at all. The verse has no retroflex ṣ anywhere, which after the last eight verses is a relief and also a trap, since the tongue has got used to curling back.

Vowel lengths: maṅgalā has three short syllables and a long one; the ṅ before g is a guttural nasal made where the g is made. Mayī is short then long. Sarvamayī and sarvaśaktimayī end identically and both endings are long.

For what to hold: the last name is the instruction, and it is unusually specific. If every mantra is her own form, then the syllables being said are not a message addressed to somebody. The traditional way of putting this is that in japa the reciter, the recitation and the deity are not three, and the Bhāvana Upaniṣad makes the same point about the diagram and the body. Chanting this verse slowly with attention on the sound itself rather than on the meaning is the practice the name describes.

The dense little word tajjalān is a compressed formula for origin, dissolution and sustenance in one breath.
